ledger.sentence: Antimotility agents are medicines that slow the bowel to treat diarrhoea, and loperamide is the member covered on this site.
ledger.note: NHS: slowing the activity of the bowel

ledger.sentence: The NHS says loperamide works by slowing the bowel so that more water is absorbed and stools firm up.
The US FDA describes loperamide as acting on opioid receptors in the gut to slow movement through the intestine.

The NHS lists severe diarrhoea after antibiotics, a flare-up of ulcerative colitis, constipation or a swollen stomach, and blood in the stool with a high temperature as situations where loperamide is not suitable.
The NHS says loperamide is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough evidence about it.
The NHS says some medicines can affect how loperamide works, including clozapine, ritonavir, quinidine, itraconazole, gemfibrozil and desmopressin.
MedlinePlus says taking more than the recommended amount of loperamide can cause serious heart problems that may be fatal.
